planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted semi-hardwood cuttings in lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun once frost danger has passed; this species is distinct from Lavandula stoechas and is grown chiefly for its unusually long, rabbit-ear flower stalks.

directions: This Iberian and North African lavender is immediately recognizable by its exceptionally long, slender flower stalks, which hold a dense dark-purple flower head topped with large, upright, butterfly-like purple bracts far above the narrow gray-green foliage. Plant in lean, fast-draining, slightly alkaline soil in full sun and avoid rich organic amendments, which encourage soft growth and winter rot. It is somewhat less cold hardy than English lavender and benefits from a gritty mulch and wind-sheltered position in the cooler end of its range. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush to maintain a tidy mound and encourage a possible second flowering later in the season.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Set out divisions or rooted cuttings in lean, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed; this is one of the fastest-spreading mat-forming thymes and can outrun less vigorous creeping species if not given room.

directions: Native to rocky Mediterranean hillsides, this vigorous mat-forming thyme spreads noticeably faster than common creeping thyme, making it useful for covering ground between stepping stones or on dry banks in a single season. Medium-green leaves are topped in late spring and early summer with unusually large, showy pink flower heads that draw heavy bee activity. Plant in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun and avoid overwatering, which causes the dense mat to rot from the center outward. Trim back hard after flowering if the planting becomes woody or bare in the middle, since it readily resprouts from the remaining runners.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; grown as an ornamental for its bracts and flowers rather than as a culinary herb.

directions: Native to western Turkey and the Aegean islands, this wiry-stemmed oregano carries slightly glaucous, blue-green oval leaves and arching sprays of rose-pink, tubular flowers that stand well clear of the foliage in summer, giving it a more open and showy habit than most culinary oreganos. Grow it in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where it performs best in rock gardens, raised beds, or containers that mimic its native rocky slopes. It is more cold-sensitive than common marjoram, so provide a sheltered site or winter protection outside its hardy range. Cut back lightly after flowering to keep the sprawling stems from becoming woody and bare.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, or propagate from cuttings; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into lean, sharply drained soil.

directions: Endemic to dry hillsides of south-central Spain, this sage forms a low mound of felted, silvery-white leaves from which tall, branching flower stems rise in a loosely tiered, candelabra-like arrangement, giving the species its name. Two-toned violet-blue flowers with pale throats open along these branched spikes over a long summer season. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since excess moisture and winter wet are far more damaging than cold. Cut the flowering stems back to the basal foliage once bloom fades to keep the clump tidy and encourage fresh growth the following year.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this eastern Mediterranean endemic is rare in cultivation and seed can be slow or uneven to germinate, so sow extra and be patient.

directions: This little-known sage from the eastern Mediterranean basin forms a low mound of textured, slightly hairy green leaves topped by short spikes of unusually large, deep magenta-purple flowers for the plant's compact size. Despite its common name it is botanically unrelated to the Phlomis species also called Jerusalem sage, and is grown instead as a true culinary-type Salvia valued mainly as a garden curiosity and pollinator plant. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, since it is intolerant of heavy or waterlogged ground. Give it a sheltered position toward the colder end of its range, as plants are still rare in general cultivation and worth protecting through winter.
